summary: Weekly check-in focused on Dedicated sizing, autoscaling policies and burst rehearsal for LuminaHealth pilot. Reviewed last week's test results (p95 latency and token throughput), discussed KV cache hit improvements, quantization options for cost reduction, and agreed next steps for a 48-hour staging burst.
transcript:
Header: Date: 2027-03-02 10:00 AM PT | Duration: 48 minutes | Recording: yes

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining! Quick roll call, we have Daniel, Priya, Samir from LuminaHealth and Ravi and me from Redwood.
[00:08] Daniel Ortega: Yeah hi, thanks Maya. Sorry for the delay, morning got blown up with a quick on-call.
[00:13] Priya Nair: Morning all.
[00:16] Ravi Patel: hey, good morning. I'll jump to the test results straight away, have screen ready -- I think we shared the spreadsheet but I'll recap.
[00:24] Maya Chen: Perfect, yeah we'd love a brief recap of the 72-hour run and the short burst yesterday.
[00:30] Ravi Patel: Ok so to summarize, steady-state traffic 20 rps, with a 15 minute ramp to 200 rps for the short burst. Results: average token throughput climbed to ~380k tokens / minute at peak, p50 latency stayed sub 120ms for small contexts, p95 drifted to 1.1s during the 2m peak window. There was a KV cache hit improvement after Priya's patch -- cache hit increased from about 38% to 61% which saved roughly 18% of token compute.
[01:05] Priya Nair: yep I rebased the cache keys to include intent hash, that knocked down repeated prefixes a bit. still some noisy sessions causing cold starts.
[01:15] Daniel Ortega: The p95 1.1s — is that within the SLA we discussed? Our user SLO is 750ms for interactive flows.
[01:24] Maya Chen: Right, p95 at 1.1s is above 750ms. A few notes: the short peak had a lot of long-context requests, around 2k tokens per request, which amplifies generation time. We can approach this two ways: route long context requests to a lower-cost tolerant path or shard capacity so interactive routes have reserved headroom.
[01:45] Samir Lowe: From security side, a reminder — we'll need audit logs for Dedicated, and KMS key usage logs. Any changes to the autoscale triggering that require elevated IAM roles need to pass our audit.
[01:56] Ravi Patel: totally agree. For Dedicated we can emit audit events to your log collector over the VPC peering. We also support customer-managed KMS, HSM in private deployments.
[02:09] Daniel Ortega: Good. Can you give a quick overview of the autoscale policy you propose?
[02:13] Ravi Patel: Sure. Current default is reactive: scale-up at 70% GPU utilization, scale-down at 30% after a 10m cool-down. For your burst pattern we suggest a hybrid policy: proactive buffer + burst pre-provisioning. That is, keep a 20% reserve on the interactive pool for headroom, and a separate burst pool that can be spun up with a priority preempt policy. The burst pool can be warmed using a static warm-up traffic generator to pre-populate KV caches and model weight pages. This reduces cold-start p95 spikes.
[02:47] Priya Nair: How long to spin up the burst pool typically? in our last test it took about 5-7 minutes to get to full capacity.
[02:56] Ravi Patel: That's in line with Dedicated instance cold start. We recommend a 5 minute pre-warm window triggered by an early signal (e.g., queued task count or ramp forecast). Also, incremental scaling with smaller increments (20% steps) reduces variance in tail latency compared to all-at-once scaling.
[03:13] Daniel Ortega: What's the cost impact of keeping that 20% reserve? we have tight budget for the pilot.
[03:20] Maya Chen: Good call — we modelled the cost. For your current throughput profile, a 20% reserve increases monthly committed spend by about 8-10% but reduces missed SLO penalties and p95 tails substantially. We included potential mitigation: use quantized model variant for background/long-context routes which reduces GPU usage ~30% with a small quality delta — that lowers the effective cost of the reserve.
[03:44] Priya Nair: can you quantify the quality delta? Clinical NLP is sensitive to hallucinations.
[03:50] Ravi Patel: For the quantized int8 variant we saw ROUGE / BLEU-style metrics drop minimally on our internal evals — for your prompts we expect negligible drift on extraction tasks but recommend keeping the main interactive route on the full-precision model.
[04:06] Samir Lowe: Also need to ensure model weights aren't exfiltrated in cache dumps — can the cache be encrypted and access audited?
[04:14] Ravi Patel: KV cache is stored ephemeral on node local and we encrypt in transit; audit events include cache population calls. For on-prem we can support additional disk-level encryption and HSM proxies.
[04:24] Maya Chen: Let's walk through a proposed rehearsal: 48-hour staging run with two scheduled bursts. Burst A is a short spike (200 rps, 15m) to validate scale-up/repopulation. Burst B is a long surge (120 rps sustained for 4 hours) to exercise autoscale and cost. We'll run with 20% interactive reserve and separate burst pool using the quantized variant for background inference. Priya, you will map your traffic routes to 'interactive' vs 'background' and we'll help route policy.
[05:01] Priya Nair: Sounds reasonable. I do have a question on the routing layer — can we route based on request headers and session attributes? Our app sets a tenant header and a workflow tag.
[05:12] Ravi Patel: Yes we support header-based routing, and can do priority tagging for tenants. You can pass a routing key to pin sessions to interactive pool. There's also an L7 filter if you need path-based rules.
[05:23] Daniel Ortega: Any failure modes we should be aware of — like when the burst pool can't allocate due to region capacity?
[05:29] Ravi Patel: Good point. We recommend a fallback policy: if burst pool unavailable, fallback to a slightly cheaper model variant that can run on smaller instances, and degrade throughput gracefully with rate-limiting and queueing. Redwood's router will auto-fallback and emit event to ops.
[05:44] Maya Chen: Ok let's capture immediate action items and owners. Also, we'd like to run a short dry run tomorrow to validate pre-warm pipeline.
[05:52] Daniel Ortega: can we do a 15-min dry run at 9am PT tomorrow? that's when our engineers are free.
[05:58] Maya Chen: works for us.
[06:00] Ravi Patel: I'll prepare a load generator script with two profiles: short spike and long ramp. I'll also include a warm-up routine that hits a set of curated prefixes to fill KV cache.
[06:12] Priya Nair: I'll share traffic histograms and the list of routes with tags by EOD today.
[06:16] Samir Lowe: I'll start the security checklist and share the contact for our infra team for VPC peering.
[06:22] Maya Chen: Great. Any other questions?
[06:24] Daniel Ortega: One more — how will you measure success for the POC? We want clear pass/fail.
[06:29] Maya Chen: We'll use success criteria: p95 <= 750ms on interactive routes during scheduled bursts, cache hit >= 60% on interactive traffic, and cost delta within 12% of baseline with reserve. If those are met during the 48-hour run, we consider pilot successful and propose next step: Dedicated commit conversation.
[06:47] Priya Nair: ok makes sense.
[06:50] Maya Chen: recap — Redwood to send autoscale YAML, load script, and updated cost model by Friday; Lumina to run 48-hour staging with two bursts and report results; schedule wrap meeting 2027-03-18. Thanks everyone!
[07:04] Daniel Ortega: Thanks all.
[07:06] End of recording.
